references.text: Describes how Jacob bought Esau's birthright, which is relevant for understanding why Jacob pretends to be Esau in Gen 27:19.
Isaac asks Esau to hunt game and prepare a dish for him so that he can bless Esau before his death, setting the stage for Jacob's deception in verse 19.
Rebekah devises a plan for Jacob on how to pretend to be Esau to receive Isaac's blessing, which leads directly to the events in verse 19.
Warns against immorality and godlessness by referring to Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal, which is the background for the conflict between Esau and Jacob.
The contrast between Jacob's false claim of being the firstborn and Esau's confirmation of the same title underscores the theme of deception and loss of identity.
Both scenes deal with the struggle and discussion over who should have the birthright and the blessing, but with different theological outcomes.
The verses form a direct narrative connection where Jacob's deception in 27:19 leads to Esau's desperate plea for a blessing in 27:38.
The verses describe respectively the planning (27:6) and execution (27:19) of the same deception, providing full understanding of the sequence of events.
The verses form a cause-and-effect chain where Jacob's deception in 27:19 directly leads to Esau's accusation of double deception in 27:36.
The verses show the connection between Jacob receiving the blessing in 27:19 and Isaac's inability to give the same gift to Esau later.
The verses describe immediate before-and-after scenes in the same event: Jacob's deception to obtain the blessing and Esau's desperate reaction to the loss.
The verses create a theological contrast between Jacob's human attempt to secure the blessing through deception (27:19) and his later recognition that everything is God's grace (32:10).
